old: The assigned note connects the decision with sales-law modification rules. UCC § 2-209 removes the need for new consideration, but duress remains available through § 1-103(b), and Comment 2 to § 2-209 requires good faith. Thus, the consideration objection associated with Alaska Packers did not exhaust the analysis. The later Restatement §§ 175–176 framework maps coerced assent and absence of reasonable alternatives to § 175, and wrongful threatened breach to § 176(1)(d). Those are explanatory comparisons, not additional holdings in this appeal.
new: The assigned note connects the decision with sales-law modification rules. UCC § 2-209 removes the need for new consideration, but duress remains available through § 1-103(b), and Comment 2 to § 2-209 requires good faith. reason: Restatement § 176(1)(d) makes a threat improper only when the threat is a breach of the duty of good faith and fair dealing under a contract with the recipient; not every threatened breach qualifies.

reason: Loral protested in writing when it gave in (July 22); what it delayed was its demand for a refund.

old: A pressured party may undo a contract if it agreed only because the other side made a wrongful threat that left it no real free choice.
new: A pressured party may undo a contract if the other side's wrongful threat forced it to agree by leaving it no real free choice.
reason: The court's test is that the party 'was forced to agree to it by means of a wrongful threat precluding the exercise of his free will'; it does not require that the threat be the only reason (Restatement § 175 comment c: substantially contributes).

old: A contract modification is voidable for economic duress when a party threatens to withhold goods owed under a contract, and the threatened party cannot obtain them from another source in time and an ordinary action for breach would be inadequate.
new: A contract modification is voidable for economic duress when a wrongful threat precluding free will, such as withholding owed goods unless a further demand is met, forces agreement, the threatened party cannot obtain the goods elsewhere in time, and an ordinary action for breach would be inadequate.
reason: Austin's test requires that the party was forced to agree by a wrongful threat precluding the exercise of free will, the threat being to withhold goods unless the other party agrees to a further demand; the rule line dropped the inducement and the link between threat and demand.

old: Later Restatement § 89 can support some modifications without new consideration, but replacement difficulty alone does not establish unforeseen circumstances supporting a fair adjustment, and § 89(c) does not automatically protect every performance of an existing duty. New York General Obligations Law § 5-1103 can remove consideration objections to qualifying signed modifications without supplying authority or eliminating duress. Uniform Commercial Code § 2-209 applies to goods modifications; a crew’s services contract is not a goods sale merely because its employer sells salmon.
new: Later Restatement § 89 can support some modifications without new consideration, but replacement difficulty alone does not establish circumstances not anticipated by the parties that would make an adjustment fair and equitable, and § 89(c) does not automatically protect every performance of an existing duty. New York General Obligations Law § 5-1103 can remove consideration objections to qualifying signed modifications without supplying authority or eliminating duress. Uniform Commercial Code § 2-209 applies to goods modifications; a crew’s services contract is not a goods sale merely because its employer sells salmon.
reason: Restatement § 89(a) asks whether the modification is 'fair and equitable in view of circumstances not anticipated by the parties when the contract was made'; comment b counts an event foreseen as a remote possibility if the contract did not adequately cover it, so 'events nobody expected' changes the test.

old: Restatement § 89, a later rule, can make some contract "modifications" (changes) binding without new consideration if fair and caused by "unforeseen circumstances," events nobody expected. Difficulty finding replacement workers alone does not qualify, and § 89(c) does not automatically protect every "performance" of a duty already owed.
new: Restatement § 89, a later rule, can make a "modification" (change) of a contract not yet fully performed binding without new consideration if it is "fair and equitable" in view of circumstances the parties did not anticipate when they contracted. An event foreseen only as a remote possibility can count if the contract did not adequately cover it. Difficulty finding replacement workers alone does not qualify, and § 89(c) does not automatically protect every "performance" of a duty already owed.

old: New York General Obligations Law § 5-1103 can remove "consideration" objections (that nothing new was exchanged) to qualifying signed, written "modifications" of a contract. But it does not give someone authority he lacked, and it does not cure duress, meaning improper pressure.
new: New York General Obligations Law § 5-1103 can remove "consideration" objections (that nothing new was exchanged) to a written "modification" of a contract signed by the party against whom it is to be enforced, or by that party's agent. But it does not give someone authority he lacked, and it does not cure duress, meaning improper pressure.
reason: N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 5-1103 protects only a writing signed by the party against whom the change is to be enforced, or by that party's agent.

Model UCC § 2-209 removes consideration as a requirement for a goods modification, but the modification must meet the Code’s test of good faith. old: The casebook compares Schwartzreich, where parties tore signatures from the old salary agreement and signed a replacement. Watkins did not require that ceremony. Later Restatement § 89 comment b criticized simultaneous rescission as a fiction and instead tested a modification’s fairness and justification directly. Its first illustration uses the cellar, unexpected rock, and nine-times rate to reach a binding modification when reasonable. That later route was not the rule Allen applied and does not erase his conclusion that mutual mistake failed. An event can leave the initial obligation intact yet support a consensual adjustment.
new: The casebook compares Schwartzreich, where parties tore signatures from the old salary agreement and signed a replacement. Watkins did not require that ceremony. Later Restatement § 89 comment b rejected simultaneous rescission as a fiction and instead asked directly whether a modification is fair and equitable in view of circumstances not anticipated when the contract was made. Its first illustration uses the cellar, unexpected rock, and nine-times rate to reach a binding modification when reasonable. That later route was not the rule Allen applied and does not erase his conclusion that mutual mistake failed. An event can leave the initial obligation intact yet support a consensual adjustment.
reason: Restatement § 89 comment b says 'That theory is rejected here'; the § 89(a) test is fair and equitable in view of circumstances not anticipated.

old: The coerced party may avoid the modification and seek appropriate recovery. Continued performance or a delay in protesting can be consistent with ongoing pressure, as in Austin.
new: The coerced party may avoid the modification and seek appropriate recovery. The coerced party must disaffirm promptly once the pressure ends. In Austin, Loral protested in writing when it gave in and could wait to demand a refund until three days after the last delivery, because further stoppages remained possible until then.
reason: Loral did not delay its protest (letter of July 22); the court required one who would recover money paid under duress to 'act promptly' and excused only the wait for the refund demand while further compulsion was possible.

reason: Restatement § 89(c) and comment d enforce a modification, otherwise not binding, to the extent justice requires because of reliance.
